https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c74g.text: Figure caption, Nobel Peace Prize winner Dmitry Muratov warns of the possibility of nuclear escalation under Putin By Steve Rosenberg BBC Russia Editor ,Â Reporting from Moscow Published 2 hours ago At the Moscow offices of newspaper Novaya Gazeta, the corridors are silent. There is an overwhelming sense of emptiness. "There is no newspaper anymore," former chief editor Dmitry Muratov tells me in an exclusive interview, published on the BBC News YouTube channel , external . Mr Muratov co-founded Novaya Gazeta more than 30 years ago. It became the flagship for hard-hitting independent journalism in Russia, shining a light on human rights abuses and high-level corruption. In 2021 Mr Muratov was joint winner of the Nobel Peace Prize for his efforts "to safeguard freedom of expression." The Nobel Committee noted that "six of [Novaya Gazeta's] journalists have been killed, including Anna Politkovskaya who wrote revealing articles on the war in Chechnya." It was recognition for courageous reporting. But it didn't protect the paper. Image source, EPA Image caption, Muratov auctioned off his Nobel Prize medal to support UNICEF's humanitarian efforts to support Ukrainian refguees "Putin issued a decree and the newspaper's printing presses were nationalised," Mr Muratov explains. "Its registration was revoked." Novaya Gazeta does retain a presence online. But only just: the authorities have blocked access to its website. It can only be accessed from abroad, or with the help of VPNs â virtual private networks used to circumvent restrictions. The newspaper's difficulties reflect the broader crackdown on free speech in Russia which has accelerated since the Kremlin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. "Most opinion leaders have been declared 'foreign agents', 'extremists' or 'terrorists'. Several hundred," says Dmitry Muratov. "Figures vary, but at a conservative estimate, since the start of Russia's 'special military operation' [in Ukraine] at least 1,500 people are now in prison having spoken out against current state policy. That's three times more than during the savage days of the KGB in the USSR." In his 1975 Nobel Peace Prize lecture dissident Andrei Sakharov listed the names of more than 120 political prisoners he was aware of in the Soviet Union. A decade later Amnesty International estimated more than 600 prisoners of conscience in the USSR. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Journalists Antonina Favorskaya, Konstantin Gabov, Sergey Karelin and Artyom Kriger were jailed on extremism charges for five and half years What the Kremlin had assumed in 2022 would be a short, successful "military operation" has become the bloodiest conflict in Europe since the Second World War. Yet a confident President Putin continues to predict victory for Russia. "There will never be 'victory'," counters Dmitry Muratov. "Because what has been going on for nearly five years â no matter how it ends â can no longer be considered a victory. "It cannot be a victory when two Slavic nations have ripped a million people to shreds. Or more than a million." "It seems to me that the situation with Ukraine now is this: you can destroy it, but you cannot conquer it. What do I mean by destroy? Continued escalation all the way to the use of a nuclear weapon." Does he really believe the Kremlin leader would use nuclear weapons in this war? "All those political experts who say 'Putin thinks this' or 'Putin is scared of that'â¦they're all charlatans," claims Dmitry Muratov. "It's in the same league as astrology. Nobody knows what's going on in Vladimir Putin's head. And I don't know. "I see things only as a journalist. I study big data. And since the beginning of the year the need to use nuclear weapons has been mentioned more than 500 times. When wackos say this, I pay no attention. But I've heard it discussed on state TV. And at the St Petersburg International Economic Forum, a state-run event, one of the speakers talked up the use of nuclear weapons as something favourable, something good." When he announced the mass invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, President Putin spoke of "ensuring the security of Russia." "Tell me, has security increased?" Dmitry Muratov asks. "With Ukrainian drones now attacking warehouses of [Russia's largest online retailer] Wildberries; with the petrol crisis, the disruption to mobile internet, the political prisoners? Has security increased, or not?" Despite opinion polls registering a fall in Vladimir Putin's domestic approval ratings, Russia's president â Mr Muratov believes - retains a tight grip on power. "Sorry, I don't believe all this talk about a split among members of the elite, about secret conspiracies. The country is run by Vladimir Putin. They're frightened of him. "And this fear is reinforced in every way by his main support base: the Federal Security Service (FSB)." As critical as he is of his own government, he has few illusions about the West. "[Putin] knows very well the true value of European leaders. On the one hand they talk to him about human rights. He laughs out loud because, with the other hand, they sign agreements â or used to sign agreements â with Russia on trading oil, gas, diamondsâ¦all that stuff. When they talk to Putin about European values, he truly laughs out loud. He knows the true value of people who preached to him those values." In Russia Mr Muratov has been designated a 'foreign agent', a label often used to punish critics of the Kremlin. 'Foreign agents' have limited rights: they're banned from teaching, from taking part in elections; if they sell their flat, they can't access the assets. The label is also designed to stigmatise, to create the sense in society of an enemy within. Yet the journalist appears reluctant to focus on the pressures he's under, preferring instead to highlight the plight of compatriots in prison. "What worries me most right now is that no one in the world is interested in the political prisoners who were first to speak out against the land grab in our neighbouring country," Dmitry Muratov explains. Image caption, Nadezhda Buyanova, a 68-year-old Ukrainian-born paediatrician sentenced to five and a half years in a penal colony for allegedly criticising the war in Ukraine at work He opens a folder and takes out a stack of large photographs: portraits of prisoners. One shows four journalists - Antonina Favorskaya, Konstantin Gabov, Sergey Karelin and Artyom Kriger â convicted and jailed on extremism charges. They'd been accused of links to the anti-corruption organisation of the late opposition leader Alexei Navalny. There's a photo of Alexei Gorinov: a city councillor jailed for "knowingly spreading false information" about the Russian military after he spoke out against the war in Ukraine. "And here's a wonderful pianist, Pavel Kushnir," says Dmitry Miratov. "An outstanding performer of Rachmaninoff and Schubert." The musician was arrested after posting anti-war videos. Dmitry Muratov holds up a second video. "And this is him in his coffin." Pavel Kushnir died in a pre-trial detention centre during a hunger strike. He was 39. The stream of photos and prison stories highlights the dangers for individuals framed as opponents of those in power. It's a reminder of the risks that public criticism of the authorities and the war carry. "Does being a Nobel Prize laureate give you at least some protection to say what you want?" I ask. "This is not a question for me," replies Mr Muratov. "Whenever you have the opportunity, ask the authorities that." There is one more photo. From April. "This is the newspaper's lawyer when she was waiting to get into the building. The police were searching our office. Thirteen hours it took. And they wouldn't let the lawyers in. Our managing editor Oleg Roldugin is now under house arrest." Dmitry Muratov paints a bleak picture of life in Russia for critics of the authorities. Yet there are moments of hope. "We live in a time when you stay quiet. But so many people support what we do. On the streets of Moscow, my colleagues and I hear only words of gratitude. They are spoken in a whisper. But what people think is very important." Related topics War in Ukraine Russia Nobel Prize Vladimir Putin Press freedom More on this story Who is Nobel Peace Prize winner Dmitry Muratov? AP Photo/Ghaith Alsayed https://theconversation.com/syria-journey-through-a-country-in-ruins-291199 https://theconversation.com/syria-journey-through-a-country-in-ruins-291199 Link copied Share article Share article Copy link Email Bluesky Facebook WhatsApp Messenger LinkedIn X (Twitter) Print article Just over a decade ago, at the height of Russia’s bombing campagn in Syria in 2015, an old friend who had spent much of his career teaching in the Middle East sent me two photographs of the city of Homs, which had taken a particularly heavy bombardment at the hands of Vladimir Putin’s warplanes. One of the pictures, which had been taken some years previously, was of a cafe on the centre of this city of 1.3 million. It was packed with smiling, well-dressed young men and women and hinted at a vibrant cafe culture in Syria’s third-largest city. The other was an aerial photograph downloaded from contemporaneous news reports which my friend confirmed was the street on which that cafe had sat. It was now nothing but rubble. This week our Insights team has published this moving account by three peace and conflict researchers who have travelled through some of Syria’s shattered cities, to observe at first hand how people have been trying to rebuild their lives since the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. They spoke with many people returning to these cities having fled the violence. They observed food stalls, cafes, repair shops and other small and medium enterprises that had sprung up amid the rubble as people began to rebuild their lives, homes and livelihoods. The researchers, from the UK’s Durham University and the Bonn International Centre for Conflict Studies, attended the wedding of a friend and recount hearing the joyous zalghouta – the traditional high-pitched ululation so characteristic of celebrations across the Arab world. As they write here: “hope and hardship coexist. So do recovery and destruction”. Or as someone told them when they visited Damascus: “We sit on the ashes, and everything remains extremely fragile.” Read more: Journeying through Syria’s shattered cities as they move from war to peace Iran’s shifting power structure Something else that remains extremely fragile is the ceasefire in Iran – if indeed it still exists in any meaningful sense. Both sides have carried out strikes this week. The US has hit what it referred to as military targets, including rocket-propelled mine launchers in the Strait of Hormuz (although it also reportedly hit a wedding party, killing several civilians and wounding many others). Iran struck at US military assets in the Gulf. Tehran is now threatening to launch cyberattacks against energy and water facilities in the US. Donald Trump, has said he has no plans to talk with Iran, claiming that the US has almost total control of the Strait of Hormuz and that the Iranian economy is close to collapse. He reiterated his call from the beginning of the conflict for the Iranian people to rise against the Islamic Republic. While there’s no sense that the regime is in any real jeopardy at present, the war has prompted some important power shifts in Iran. Andreas Krieg, a Middle East specialist at King’s College London, explains who’s who in the struggle to control Iran and what that might mean for the future of negotiations with the US. Read more: War has shifted how power works in Iran Putin’s paranoia about Britain One of the policy approaches taken by Keir Starmer as prime minister which his successor Andy Burnham is clearly keen to continue is the UK’s stance as a key ally of Ukraine. Burnham’s first, and so far only, overseas visit since moving into Downing Street has been to Ukraine, where he told President Volodymyr Zelensky that “Britain is 100% behind you”. Predictably, this drew a harsh response from the Kremlin, several of whose leading lights issued threats that the deeper the UK’s involvement in the war “the higher price it will pay”. Historian Peter Whitewood of York St John University believes the messaging coming out of Putin’s proxies recently echo a familiar theme . Russia has repeatedly accused the UK of being something of a ringleader in ganging up on Russia. Whitewood points to a series of episodes in the 1920s, when Britain threw its weight behind Poland in its struggle to remain independent from the Soviets. Then, the Kremlin’s line was – as it is now – that Britain was “always striving to push others instead of itself into military actions against us”. As one Soviet diplomat observed, the Kremlin was inclined to see “the malevolent hand of the British government everywhere”. Given this was Stalin’s personal belief, there wasn’t much mileage in suggesting it was misguided and it wasn’t until the rise of Nazi Germany that Britain was knocked off its podium as the Soviet Union’s main bogeyman. Read more: Moscow has a long history of paranoia about Britain’s support for Russia’s enemies The tragic fate of a Nepalese village Thousands of people are still missing after the devastating floods that swept through Nepal last week, while the death toll from the disaster continues to mount. One settlement particularly hard hit was the village of Khalte, close to the Trishuli River in northern Nepal. Khalte was located on flat, sandy and gravel-heavy soil right next to the river. Heaven Crawley , Author provided (no reuse) This village of around 5,750 people included 257 families who had been displaced in the disaster of 2015, when Nepal was rocked by a 7.8-magnitude earthquake. Heaven Crawley, a researcher from Coventry University, spent time working with families there in September 2019 as part of a research project looking at how renewable energy could improve people’s lives. As she writes here , the local people were well aware of how precarious their village was as it was critically vulnerable to flooding from the Trishuli, which repeatedly flowed into Khalte, particularly during monsoon season. The urgency of finding somewhere safer was further brought home in 2025, when a glacial lake outburst sent floodwaters flowing into Nepal from Tibet. Now Khalte no longer exists. It was completely swept away in the flooding of August 26. Scores of people are missing. Crawley believes that this terrible tragedy must be taken seriously as a lesson about the urgency of heeding these climate warnings. Read more: Nepal floods: Khalte residents knew the river could take their camp – and then it did Inside North Korea’s ‘shadow fleet’ Shadow fleets are the outlaws of the ocean. They are used by countries such as Russia, Iran and North Korea to evade sanctions and are among the reasons why some of the world’s conflicts seem so intractable. In the latest episode of The Conversation Weekly, Justin Hastings, a professor of international relations at the University of Sydney, describes the tactics that North Korea uses to disguise the identities of its shadow ships – and why it has got away with it for so long. There’s a superb multimedia piece to go with it, with vivid graphics illustrating the way in which shadow fleets go about hiding their identities. Photograph: Yuki Iwamura/AP Mississippi Mississippi grand jury decides not to charge anyone in death of Nolan Wells Jury report says ‘no credible evidence’ points to criminal conduct related to death of Mississippi teen after boat outing with friends on 4 July Adria R Walker Tue 22 Sep 2026 10.55 EDT Last modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 10.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A grand jury made a unanimous decision late Monday night to not bring criminal charges against anyone in the mysterious death of Nolan Wells, a Mississippi teen who died after a boat outing with friends on 4 July. The Jackson county, Mississippi grand jury, which met from 14 September to 18 September, issued 132 subpoenas during its investigation, considered evidence from 43 witnesses and investigators, and reviewed an independent investigation by Wells’ family. They also considered physical and digital evidence, including mobile phone data and forensic reports, photographs, videos and GPS data. A copy of the grand jury report was posted online by the Jackson county district attorney’s office, which said that there was “no credible evidence to support the public allegations that any persons who rode to or from Horn Island on July 4, 2026 … engaged in any criminal conduct related to the death of Mr Wells”. “The allegations against the occupants of the Triton, the Palm Beach, and the Tideline [boats that traveled to the island] are not based in truth, and are solely the result of public clamor and private malice,” the report says. Wells’ case drew national attention, with many speculating about what happened and suspecting that the teen’s disappearance and death may have been racially motivated. Wells, who was Black while the friends with whom he was last seen were white, was also the only friend in the group who didn’t return from the trip to the barrier island that day. Per the grand jury report, Wells chose to stay behind on the island and come back later with another group as it was “not unusual or suspicious for individuals to return from the island on boats they did not travel … on”. Wells’ family, however, has consistently pushed back on this claim, suggesting that it is not something that the teen would have done. “We always taught him that if you go with a group, you stay with a group,” said Elmore Wonsley, his father, during the Good Morning America appearance in July. “If you go with five, you come back with five. Do not separate from the group. Because I always said: ‘Safety is in numbers.’ So he knew to stay with this group, so why would he split from the group? I don’t know.” View image in fullscreen Christine Wells-Wonsley, the mother of Nolan Wells, speaks during a press conference on 22 July 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. Photograph: Scott Olson/Getty Images Wells’ family, through their attorney Ben Crump, announced the results of an autopsy performed by Dr Roger A Mitchell Jr, a forensic pathologist the team hired, in late July. Mitchell found that Wells had “sustained recent unexplained blunt force injuries to the back of the head and additional areas of his back”. Both the independent autopsy and the state’s chief medical examiner said that the cause and manner of Wells’ death were undetermined. “Drowning is a diagnosis of exclusion,” the grand jury report said. They also found that “the position of, the condition of, time of discovery, and location of Mr Wells’ body is consistent with drowning”. The grand jury found that Wells was not the only Black person on Horn Island on 4 July, and that “false assertions have led to misidentification, speculation, and rumors concerning the death of Mr Wells”, according to the report. “The family, the Crump team, and anyone close to Nolan knew that his disappearance and death were not the result of racial hate or violence,” said Angel Myers McIlrath, Jackson county district attorney, in a video posted on social media alongside the grand jury report on Monday. The 23 grand jurors included 13 men and 10 women. Twelve of the jurors were white, five were Black, two were Hispanic, two were Native American, one was Asian and one was identified as “other”, according to information released by the district attorney’s office. “There is absolutely no evidence to support the allegations that Nolan’s disappearance and death were racially motivated,” Myers McIlrath said in the video. Crump, the civil rights attorney who is representing the Wells family, said the grand jury’s decision is an attempt “to close the chapter on Nolan Wells’ death without getting to the truth”. Wells’ legal team is releasing Mitchell’s full report and requesting that the Jackson County district attorney do the same with the state’s medical examiner’s report. Additionally, they are calling on the district attorney’s office to keep the investigation open and active. Crump said that the report “leaves us with more questions than answers”. “Mississippi’s own pathologist found two bruises on the back of this young man’s head and informed investigators of them early in this investigation,” Crump said in a statement. “An independent autopsy documented traces of blood and recent blunt force injuries to the back of Nolan’s head and his back. To this day, not one person has explained how they got there. “Dr Mitchell also wrote that the record does not establish whether Nolan entered the water on his own or was forced, or whether he was conscious when he went in. We don’t know how Nolan died, and neither does the state of Mississippi. Mississippi must keep investigating, and if it will not pursue this to the end, the Department of Justice should. ” There is no statute of limitations for homicide cases in Mississippi, something the grand jury report noted. If any evidence were to emerge that suggests that Wells’ death was not accidental, it should be referred to the grand jury for consideration.
